title: WION Ai EDU Summit explores AI’s impact on learning & skills
excerpt: The WION Ai EDU Summit 2026 brought together policymakers, educators, technology leaders and industry experts in Bengaluru on September 24 to discuss the impact of artificial intelligence on education, learning and future skills. The summit opened with Sri Madhu Bangarappa, Cabinet Minister for School Education and Literacy, Government of Karnataka, who spoke about the need for young people to understand AI while also developing personality and other human capabilities. Naganand Doraiswamy, managing partner & founder, Ideaspring Capital, and co-chairman, Vision Group for Startups, ITBT, Government of Karnataka, delivered the keynote on “Building the Next Decade of Innovation: AI, Startups & the Future of Karnataka”. He discussed the use of AI across industries and education and Karnataka's role in the startup and innovation ecosystem. The first panel, ‘AI@Work: The Future Logs In’, focused on the adoption of AI in business. The discussion covered applications including predictive AI in airport operations, data analysis, creator discovery, content analysis, market intelligence and decision-making. The second panel, ‘The AI Class Act: The Future of Learning’, examined how AI is changing education. The discussion covered the importance of independent thinking, reading, critical thinking, foundational skills and personalised learning, while also considering the continuing role of teachers and mentors. The final panel, ‘Funding the Future’, brought together investors and founders to discuss AI, entrepreneurship and responsible innovation. The discussion included AI's role in productivity and customer experience, as well as issues around human oversight, guardrails and the responsibilities of investors, founders and governments. The summit concluded with a live Carnatic music performance by musician and singer Vinay Sharva. Speaking on the summit, Raktim Das, CEO, Zee Media, said: “The future of education and learning is being shaped by the rapid evolution of Artificial Intelligence, creating new possibilities for how we learn, innovate and prepare for tomorrow. The WION Ai EDU Summit 2026 brought together diverse perspectives on how AI can transform education, businesses, skills and the wider innovation ecosystem. As India moves towards becoming a global AI powerhouse, nurturing AI-ready talent, accelerating innovation and enabling wider adoption of AI will be critical to shaping the next decade of growth.” (afaqs! got this information in a press release)

title: IACC Summit Unites 100+ Leaders to Shape India’s AI‑Ready Digital Infrastructure
excerpt: Over 100 business, policy, and technology leaders gathered in Hyderabad at the Indo-American Chamber of Commerce inaugural Summit to address critical infrastructure needs across Data Centers, AI demand, GCC Expansion, Cyber Resilience, Green energy, and cloud innovation The Indo-American Chamber of Commerce (IACC) hosted its inaugural Digital Infrastructure Summit 2026 in Hyderabad on Friday, drawing over 100 top business, technology, and policy leaders. The summit set out to chart a roadmap for the robust, secure digital infrastructure to power India’s next wave of AI innovation and digital growth. Organized by the Andhra Pradesh & Telangana Branch of the IACC, with support from CtrlS Datacenters as the Presenting Partner, the summit brought together key voices across industry, government, and finance to align on a shared vision for India’s digital growth. In her welcome speech, Dr. Sreedevi Devireddy, Chairperson, IACC Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, said, “India is on the cusp of an unprecedented digital revolution, where next-generation infrastructure will act as the ultimate catalyst for hyper-scale innovation. Looking beyond simple capacity, we are pioneering a sustainable future, scaling world-class data centers, expanding Global Capability Centers (GCCs), fortifying cybersecurity, and deploying secure, AI-ready technologies. The Indo-American Chamber of Commerce is proud to unite visionary leaders from industry, government, and finance to bridge critical gaps and forge high-impact partnerships. Hyderabad and Telangana are uniquely positioned to power this ecosystem, and this inaugural IACC Digital Infrastructure Summit 2026 marks the launchpad for a sustained, forward-looking movement.” Sreedevi added. The inaugural session laid a strong strategic foundation for the day’s deliberations on India’s digital infrastructure growth. Mr. Srikanth Badiga, Group Director of Phoenix Group, Chairman of SEZEPC (Ministry of Commerce & Industry, GoI), and Director NEC, IACC, delivered the Theme Address, setting the tone for India’s digital scaling journey. Mr. Chandra Shekhar Sarma G, CISO & Director of Compliance at CtrlS Datacenters delivered the Opening Keynote on infrastructure security, followed by a Special Address from Mr. S. Purnachandra Rao, Former National President of IACC and Managing Director of Global Infovision Pvt. Ltd. The summit featured distinguished leadership from both government and diplomacy. Ms. Laura Williams, Consul General at the U.S. Consulate General in Hyderabad, addressed the gathering as Guest of Honour, emphasizing bilateral technology and trade collaboration. Addressing the IACC Summit, Ms. Laura Williams said that Mission 500, COMPACT, TRUST, and Pax Silica are not abstract frameworks — they are direct opportunities for investment, supply-chain partnership, and market access, especially here in Telangana and across South India. As Ambassador Gor said: Our two countries have always built the strongest relationship from the ground up through entrepreneurs, engineers, and manufacturers who see opportunities in partnership rather than competition. Chandra Shekhar Sarma G, CISO & Director, Compliance, CtrlS Datacenters , stated, “ India’s digital transformation is entering a defining phase, with digital infrastructure evolving from an enabler to the foundation of the digital economy. The convergence of AI, cloud, hyperscale computing, edge and data-intensive applications is reshaping infrastructure needs. The next phase will be defined by speed to capacity, high-density compute, resilient connectivity, reliable power, sustainability and intelligent scalability ." Keynotes & Strategic Panel Highlights The business sessions kicked off with an insightful keynote on "The Future of India’s AI & Cloud Landscape" by Mr. Anil Nama, CIO of CtrlS Datacenters Ltd., followed by a dynamic session on "The Build & Scale Journey" by Mr. Anil Pinapala, Managing Director of Vivifi India Finance Private Limited. The summit’s technical agenda centered on two high-impact panel discussions:Building India's AI & Digital Infrastructure Capital: Moderated by Mr. Varma Konala (Co-Founder & CEO, Mahanim India), this panel brought together Mr. Shyam Menon (Co-Founder & General Partner, Bharat Innovation Fund), Mr. Rahul Dhar (President - Global Datacenter Operations, CtrlS Datacenters Ltd.), and Ms. Padmini Gopalakrishnan (VP Software Engineering, Agrani Labs) to discuss ecosystem enablers, venture capital, and local scaling. Powering the Digital Economy — Resilience, Reliability, Security & Green Transformation: Moderated by Mr. Srini Reddy (EVP - Service Delivery, CtrlS Datacenters Ltd.), expert panelists including Dr. Paravastu Rambabu (Chief Sustainability Officer, Greenko Group), Mr. Krishna Sastry Pendyala (Partner Cybersecurity, EY), and Ms. Annapurna Kuchibhatla (CTO, Bajaj Electronics) explored the intersection of clean power, sustainability, and airtight cyber resilience in hyper-scale data centers. About the Indo-American Chamber of Commerce (IACC): Established in 1968, the Indo-American Chamber of Commerce (IACC) is the apex bilateral chamber synergizing India–U.S. economic engagement. Founded by Ambassador Chester Bowles alongside prominent industry leaders of the era, the IACC works continuously to deepen economic ties and trade between the two nations. Today, the IACC boasts a pan-India presence with over 1,500 members representing a wide cross-section of Indian and U.S. industries. First Published at www.IndianWeb2.com

During this period, the cooperative's production stats included 21.34 lakh metric tonnes of urea and 12.39 lakh metric tonnes of ammonia. Additionally, wholly owned subsidiaries demonstrated remarkable production achievements, alongside plans for expansion with two new plants underway in Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh.

title: From Crop Pests to Sick Cattle: These Farmers Are Using AI To Get Answers In Their Language
excerpt: This article has been published in partnership with the Gates Foundation. In Gujarat’s Ajarpura village, Gayatriben knew something was wrong when one of her buffaloes kept banging its head against a tree. In another place called Ishnav (Palaj),Charmiben was trying to understand why a cow was not growing properly even after being dewormed. For farmers, questions like these often require quick answers. Today, both women can turn to an artificial intelligence system and ask in their native language. Across India, AI is finding new ways to support farmers, from crop and weather advisories to cattle care and access to agricultural services. The Better India explored the Gates Foundation’s 2026 Goalkeepers Report, spoke to farmers and technology leaders, and looked at initiatives such as Maharashtra’s MahaVISTAAR and Amul’s Sarlaben to understand how AI is being shaped around farmers’ everyday needs, and what it could mean for making useful, personalised information more accessible at the grassroots. The right advice can save a whole crop For Dipali Kalbhor, a smallholder farmer and entrepreneur from Maharashtra, farming has been a journey of setbacks and second chances. After a failed poultry venture, she rebuilt her livelihood through beekeeping, growing from 30 bee boxes to more than 1,000 today. Kalbhor tells The Better India that one of her biggest lessons has been that farmers need both a strong team and access to the right information. She discovered MahaVISTAAR during an agricultural training session and now uses it for crop prices, weather, pest control and government schemes. View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Better India (@thebetterindia) Its fertiliser calculator has been particularly useful, helping her reduce fertiliser use by around 15%, she says. She also uses the platform to check local crop prices and connect with agricultural officials, calling it a tool she consults “at least two or three times a day.” She also used it for guidance on raising 10,000 mulberry saplings in a nursery, information about a vermicompost scheme and availing contact with government officers. How Sarlaben helps dairy farmers In Gujarat, Amul has introduced Sarlaben, an AI assistant that offers dairy farmers guidance on cattle health, feeding, breeding, vaccinations,offering dairy farmers guidance on cattle health, feeding, breeding, vaccinations and government schemes in Gujarati. “One of our buffaloes wouldn’t stop banging his head on a tree. Before, I’d have to go through the cooperative, pay Rs 150 for a vet visit, then wait for him to get the issue resolved. Now, I just call Sarlaben,” Gayatriben says. Sarlaben's inclusive approach ensures that even farmers with limited digital literacy can benefit from AI-driven insights. Sarlaben suggested itching around the animal’s horns could be the reason and advised cleaning the area with oil and applying turmeric and oil. “And it worked!” she says. Meenaben faced a more serious situation when a cow was about to give birth and the calf was not emerging. Sarlaben connects with Amul’s databases to provide real-time advice on animal health, breeding, feeding, and veterinary care. “We thought we’d lose her. She was about to give birth, but the calf wasn’t coming. Panicking, we called Sarlaben.” The system helped them recognise the seriousness of the situation and connect with a specialist. The calf did not survive, but the cow did. SarlabenAI helped the farmer understand when specialist intervention was needed. ‘My cows are family to me’ For Charmiben, the challenge is simple: animals cannot say what hurts. “My cows are family to me,” she says. “But at home, my children can say, ‘Mummy, my stomach hurts.’ My cows can’t tell me when something’s wrong, no?” So when she is unsure, she says, “Now, I just ask Sarlaben.” View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Better India (@thebetterindia) According to Ajay Sheth, HOD IT at Amul, Sarlaben draws on information Amul already holds about farmers and their cattle. “Sarlaben recognises farmers by their mobile number,” he explains. The system connects their questions to “the data Amul already has about their animals”. “So it’s never generic advice,” he says. Instead, it can be “specific to your cow, backed by years of Amul’s dairy research.” Language shapes that experience too. “When I first spoke to Sarlaben, I thought she was a real person. Her Gujarati was better than mine. I couldn’t believe I was talking to AI!” Gayatriben says. Meenaben adds, “Earlier, when a cow came into heat, we had to call the cooperative. Now, Sarlaben tracks the heat cycle, shows me technicians, and helps book the experts instantly.” When one of Charmiben’s cows was not growing properly despite being dewormed, she provided its name and identification number and received guidance on what to feed it. “And it worked!” she says. For AI to help farmers, it first has to understand them The Gates Foundation’s 2026 Goalkeepers Report , Make This Matter: AI, Equity, and the Choice We Can’t Delay , identifies language, local context and access as central challenges to making AI equitable. More than 90% of the data used to train early large language models came from English-language sources, the report says. India has 22 scheduled languages, along with hundreds of other languages and dialects. In agriculture, a misunderstanding can influence what a farmer sprays, feeds, plants or harvests. The report argues that AI tools need to work in the languages people speak and be built with the people who rely on them. One of the Goalkeepers Champions for 2026, Prof Ganesh Ramakrishnan, an IIT Bombay professor and a principal investigator and board member of BharatGen, an Indian multilingual AI initiative, says AI cannot simply be built elsewhere and translated later. Prof Ganesh Ramakrishnan says, it is very important for researchers to innovate with people, and not just for people. “Does the model think the way an Indian, or more specifically, an Assamese, or someone who is in a remote part ofin South India would think?” he asks. He describes a woman in a Tamil Nadu kitchen trying to access information while a pressure cooker whistles in the background, showing how technology must work within real lives. “It’s very important for us to innovate with people, and not just for people,” he says. He calls the end user a “co-inventor”. When AI becomes an everyday farming assistant Debjani Ghosh, a 2026 Goalkeepers Champion recognised for her work on human-centric AI, imagines farmers waking up to weather information , what it could mean for their crop and whether action is needed. Ghosh champions India’s 490 million informal workers—from street vendors to farmers—who are often invisible in global AI conversations and risk being left behind. “You open your phone, and you have all the information with respect to weather, rain, not rain, what does this mean for your crop, should you take any steps,” she says. “It will be a voice message; you don’t even have to read, you can listen and understand.” Debjani Ghosh, a 2026 Goalkeepers Champion envisions AI that works in farmers’ languages and fits into everyday life. For Ghosh, that is what it means for technology to become “invisible”. “We have to make life easy for people,” she says. “We have to make it easy for people to earn a livelihood. We have to make it easy for people to live a better life.” For farmers, that promise will depend on whether AI can understand their questions, recognise their local context and respond in a language they actually speak. As the Gates Foundation’s Goalkeepers Report emphasises, acting now to build AI that is inclusive and accessible can help ensure that this technology becomes a force for greater equity, and that those who stand to benefit most are not left behind.
